newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Shaky Austria coalition to meet over bank sale.
newsitem.headline: Shaky Austria coalition to meet over bank sale.

text.p: Growing conflict between Austria's two coalition parties took on fresh urgency on Thursday as Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats called for an emergency meeting to be brought forward to the weekend.

The controversial privatisation of Austria's second biggest bank, Creditanstalt-Bankverein, has plunged the government of Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party into its biggest crisis since a snap election in December 1995.
An emergency meeting of coalition leaders had been scheduled for Monday but Social Democrat chief whip Peter Kostelka said his party was prepared to bring the session forward to the weekend.

"We've told them we're prepared to meet on either Saturday or Sunday, but have not yet received a reply," Kostelka told reporters at the Social Democrat's annual convention in the southern spa town of Bad Tatzmannsdorf.
A response from the People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel was expected within the next few hours, Kostelka added.

Political analysts said the Social Democrats would try to engineer a deal at the meeting to solve differences over the sale of Creditanstalt -- once the bankers of the Habsburg imperial family and still considered a conservative fiefdom.

The Social Democrats are well aware that their conservative partners have held a series of talks with far-right opposition leader Joerg Haider over the privatisation ahead of an emergency session of parliament next Tuesday.

Rightwinger Haider, who has made strong electoral gains in recent years but is frozen out of power by the coalition alliance, told a news conference: "We have already had several rounds of talks with (People's Party Economic Minister Johann) Farnleitner and his experts."

Haider, out to exploit the split within the government, said the far right and conservatives had found common ground on a number of points regarding the sale of the flagship bank but declined to give details.

The People's Party objects to the prospect of Creditanstalt being taken over by rival Bank Austria, which is indirectly controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna and part-owned by the state.

The conservatives, who could muster a majority in parliament if supported by Haider's far-right Freedom Party, would like to see the bank sold to an international consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali.
With the risk of the parliamentary session turning into a showdown between the two ruling parties, coalition leaders may try to defuse the crisis at the weekend meeting.
One way to break the impasse would be an offer from the Social Democrats to privatise Bank Austria over the next few years, one political source said.
Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima, who has sole responsibility for choosing the Creditanstalt buyer, said he hoped the conservatives would not force a government breakdown.
"That would mean fresh elections and the only one to profit from it would be Haider," he told the magazine News.

Haider's party scored nearly 28 percent in European elections last October, just a few thousand votes behind the two big parties which have ruled Austria alone or together since the end of World War Two.
